events.text: A herald of the Celestial Ministries finds you in the colonnade of your own temple. The mortals of your domain are conspiring, the herald says: priests and kings and the guilds of the market, together, in secret, against heaven's peace. Marshal Cheon Mu wants it broken before it grows teeth. "You were prayed to by those people," the herald adds. "You will know where they meet."

effects.log: You take the sealed slip. It weighs more than paper should.

choices.text: Take the order, and mean to warn them

effects.log: You take the slip with a bow, and the herald goes away satisfied. You do not feel satisfied.

choices.text: Let it go to another god

effects.log: You hand the slip back. The herald raises one eyebrow and finds another name.

events.text: The herald hesitates over your name on the slip. "The Book of Fates says your soul stood with the mortals once," the herald says quietly, "at the last gate they held. The Ministries thought this order would show us what you are now."

choices.text: Pass the test and hunt them

effects.log: You take the order, and the herald is visibly relieved. Whatever you were, you are acting like a god.

choices.text: Fail the test on purpose, secretly

effects.log: You take it with a steady hand. Every line of it, you promise yourself, will be read twice and obeyed once.
You refuse it to the herald's face. The Ministries will remember that, and so will you.

events.text: Dalmi of the Last Candle, a hearth-goddess whose temples are mostly one room and one fire, catches your sleeve in the corridor after the order is read. "They are only trying to keep their children warm," she whispers. "If you go down, go down as their friend. Please."

effects.log: She squeezes your hand once and lets go. Her palm is as warm as a loaf.

choices.text: Shake her off and take the order

effects.log: Her hand falls away. The order is heavier than you expected, and quieter.

choices.text: Tell her you will stay out of it

effects.log: She nods as if that is also a kind of answer, and goes back to her candle.

events.text: Another god takes the order to the domains below. In the Celestial halls they say the mortals are as good as finished. You watch the mist roll over the shrines of your own domain, and do not join the toasts.

effects.log: The nectar is excellent and the room is full, and you have never felt so little part of either.
She does not ask you anything. You sit by her fire until the toasts are over.

events.text: Young gods of the Thunder Ministry queue at your door to join the hunt. Most have never been to a mortal market, or seen a roof being thatched. They ask what the faithful are like, and you find you have no easy answer.

effects.log: They write it down. You wish, a moment later, that you had said something else.
Half of them look pleased and half look as though you had told them the sky was kind.

events.text: You go down into your own domain by night and break one of the league's meeting halls in an hour. Its keepers scatter across the fields. You let them scatter. The order was to break the hall, and the hall is broken.

effects.log: The tally-sticks make a small bright fire. Whatever they counted is gone.
You slip a stick into your sleeve. It is notched with the offerings of a village that still prays to you.

events.text: The hall was a trap. The mortals have strung old prayers into wards, and every prayer is in your own name, and the wards drag at you like hands. You get back above the cloud with your robe scorched and your name still ringing in your ears.

effects.log: The prayers are badly written and very sincere. Nothing you have ever met has been stronger.
The Ministries file it as a success. Your lie is only a small one, and it fits the paperwork neatly.

events.text: You come down quietly, in a farmer's plain coat, and walk among your own worshippers for a season so that the league will not know your face when the hunt comes. The bread on the festival tables is better than the bread of heaven.

effects.log: You eat three slices. A grandmother pats your arm and says you look thin.
The couriers carry candles in their lanterns, never lamps. You file the oddity away.

events.text: You copy the Ministries' hunting plans by lamplight and slip them into bundles of votive paper that go down to the temples as offerings. Each bundle is addressed to a worshipper who does not exist. Every one of them reaches the league.

choices.text: Use Dalmi's shrine as a drop

effects.log: Her hearth takes the bundles and gives out only warmth. She never asks what is in them.
You walk the plans down the mountain in a pilgrim's pack. The league's watchers hold their breath and take them.

events.text: A hunting party leaves the Ministries at dawn. You take it on a long detour through weather you have brewed yourself, over the cold sea first and then the dry plains. By the time it reaches your domain, the league has moved on.

choices.text: Apologise to the hunters for the weather

effects.log: The hunters are too wet to hold a grudge. One of them sneezes at you, reproachfully.
The party blames the season. You blame nothing in particular.

events.text: You try to turn a hunt aside, and the hunt's captain turns with you, spear down. You escape into the fog banks, and spend a week explaining your bruises as the result of an unfortunate encounter with a river-spirit.

effects.log: It is a good story. The river-spirit, informed, says it would never have thought of it.

choices.text: Go to Dalmi's fire to heal

effects.log: She binds your hand with warm cloth and asks you nothing, and the bruises ease by morning.

events.text: You become the most dutiful god of the Celestial Ministries for a season: first at every audience, loudest at every toast to the Marshal, severe in every council on the stubbornness of mortals. It is a role, and you play it well enough to frighten yourself.

effects.log: Marshal Cheon Mu raises his own cup to you, and the room approves. You raise your cup and do not taste it.
Your speech is applauded by gods who do not notice that it contains no actual argument.

events.text: Dalmi of the Last Candle shows you her shrine's hearth, with a dozen small offerings on its ledge: a bowl of millet, a folded cloth, a child's tooth. "They bring these every winter," she says. "Not a one of them asks for anything. I keep wishing someone would teach them to."

choices.text: Help her bless this year's offerings

effects.log: Each small offering warms in your hands as you bless it. She pretends she is not crying.

choices.text: Tell her they do ask, in their own way

effects.log: She looks at the millet and the cloth and the tooth, and you see her change her mind.

events.text: Dalmi is summoned before Censor-General Gwang of the Ministries and comes back pale. Someone has been sending votive paper to the temples below, the Censor told her. She looks at you across the corridor, and does not ask.

effects.log: She takes the news like a woman receiving a letter she has long expected. She presses your hand and leaves.
She walks on. Her candle is lit when you pass her shrine that night, a very small flame.

events.text: The herald Yun Hwaseol passes you in a colonnade and stops. She has the acolyte she took from a mortal temple with her: grown now, in a god's white sleeves, carrying her scrolls. The acolyte looks at you as if trying to remember a dream.

choices.text: Ask the acolyte if they are content

effects.log: The acolyte hesitates. "I am learning to be," they say, which is an answer, and not a bad one.

choices.text: Say nothing in front of the herald

effects.log: Yun Hwaseol nods and moves on. The acolyte glances back once, then twice.

events.text: The mortals' wards strike back at the hunters. A thunder-barge comes home from your domain with its sails torn to ribbons, its crew unable to fly for a season. Marshal Cheon Mu wants to know how worshippers learned to do that.

choices.text: Say they are cleverer than we think

effects.log: The Marshal grunts. It is as close as he comes to admitting you may be right.
The Marshal accepts it. You wonder whether he believes it either.

events.text: The Censor-General's inquisitors go through the Celestial halls room by room, looking for whoever has been sending votive paper below. They search your quarters twice. They find nothing either time, and they apologise the second time, which is how you know it is dangerous.

effects.log: They drink your tea and compliment its jasmine. You say a quiet prayer to a god who does not exist.
You complain to the Marshal in the hearing of half the halls. It buys you a month of peace and a certain reputation.

events.text: You see Priestess Ok Seoljin, who kept the league's ledger of offerings, in the Celestial halls, of all places, in mortal silk, being thanked by the Censor-General's steward. The league below has lost its records and three of its speakers. She bows to you as one traitor to another.

effects.log: You bow, correctly and no lower. Your pulse is the loudest thing in the corridor.

choices.text: Warn the league what she sold

effects.log: You send a message down in a dream of a candle. By morning, the league has changed its meeting places.

events.text: A mortal priestess named Ok Seoljin is brought before the Censor-General in chains of light. She was selling the Ministries' plans to the league, the steward says, and the league's plans to the Ministries. She looks at you across the hall, and you understand that she could say your name.

effects.log: You look at your sleeve. She says nothing. You will wonder for years why.
You hold them. She gives you the smallest nod and keeps your secret to the end.

events.text: Your hunters gather on the cloud's rim, ready to fall on the Gate of Prayers at dawn. Below, through the breaks, you can see the faithful's fires, thousands of them, laid out like a city of lanterns that was not there yesterday.

effects.log: You count until your eyes ache. You stop at a number you do not say aloud.
The stone sings against the blade. For a little while it drowns the sound of the fires.

events.text: Tomorrow the Marshal's hunters fall on the Gate of Prayers, and tonight you are the only god who knows what is waiting for them. Dalmi finds you on the cloud's rim and stands beside you without a word, small and warm in the cold.

choices.text: Ask her to go below if it goes wrong

effects.log: She promises. Her candle goes out on the cloud for a moment, then lights again.

choices.text: Tell her nothing, to keep her safe

effects.log: She watches your face and decides to be kept safe. It is a kindness neither of you will mention.

events.text: Your hunters fall on the Gate of Prayers at dawn, and by noon the league is broken. The Celestial halls hold a feast in your name. In the middle of it Dalmi leaves without a word, and in the morning the one-room shrine on the hill has no candle.

effects.log: You eat and are praised, and the food is perfect, and you do not taste it.
You find her at the foot of the hill, with a candle in each hand, walking down toward the mortals. She does not turn back.

events.text: The faithful hold the Gate of Prayers. Their wards drag your hunters out of the sky like hooks pulling kites, and you come back up through the cloud with your order unfulfilled and your sleeves in strips. The Celestial halls will talk about it for ten thousand years.

effects.log: The Marshal listens with a stone face, and thanks you for your honesty with a coldness that does not quite hide respect.
You swear it in the Marshal's hall, loudly. The oath rings off the pillars, and whatever you meant by it, it is said.

events.text: The Marshal's hunters fall into the trap you warned the league of, and the league wins. In the halls above they blame the weather, the wards, the stars. Dalmi finds you on the cloud's rim and presses a small flame into your palm, in a cup of clay. It is still lit.

choices.text: Carry it down to a hearth

effects.log: You take it to the first shrine you see. The fire spreads to the lamp, and the lamp, to the village.
You cup your hands over it. It warms them all the way up the stairs.

events.text: The league is crushed, and Priestess Ok Seoljin, or someone like her, has given the Censor-General your name. The Ministries do not punish a god openly. They simply stop seeing you: no seat at the feasts, no answer at the doors, no reply to your offerings.

effects.log: She opens the shrine door before you knock, and sets a second bowl at her hearth.
You walk the whole length of the Celestial hall with your chin level. Nobody sees you walk it. You walk it anyway.

events.text: A truce is signed at the Gate of Prayers below and sealed in the Celestial halls above: the gods will not descend uninvited, and the faithful will not raise their wards against the sky. You are among the few gods who sign without holding their breath.

effects.log: The ink dries quickly. The pen, you note, does not feel any heavier than usual.
You raise cups of plain tea. It is the best toast of the age.

events.text: Years later, the Celestial halls still argue about the war with the faithful at every banquet. Young gods who were not there ask what the mortals were like. Everyone turns to you.

effects.log: You tell it plain. When you are done, a very young god asks if they can visit a village.
You talk about the harvest. The young gods look disappointed, and a little older.

events.text: The Celestial archive keeps a roll of every soul that ever raised a hand against heaven. A clerk finds yours, goes pale, and leaves to fetch someone. When you ask what it says, the clerk reads aloud: "Held the last gate. Won."

effects.log: The clerk smiles back, uncertainly, as if it had never occurred to anyone to be happy about this roll.

choices.text: Ask to see the rest of it

effects.log: The rest is two pages in a very neat hand, and ends with a drawing of a candle.

events.text: An elderly minister of the Ministries greets you warmly, as an old friend, and thanks you for a service you do not remember: the night the mortals' league was delivered to heaven. The court remembers your soul fondly. You are not sure you want them to.

effects.log: The minister beams and presses a gift into your hands. You do not look at it.

choices.text: Say you are not that soul any more

effects.log: The minister does not understand. You hope, someday, that a few others will.

events.text: Dalmi's shrine is still here, older and warmer, and its hearth has grown a second room. A young caretaker tends it now. When you walk in, the caretaker looks up and says: "She said someone would come back to see the candle."

choices.text: Kneel and help with the kindling

effects.log: The kindling takes at once. The caretaker says nothing, and offers you tea.
"She went down to the villages," the caretaker says. "She said she was going to ask them for something."

events.text: At noon the sky over the great school splits like cloth, and a tall figure in white steps down through the rent as if down a stair. The small gods' messenger, the people name it afterwards. It walks past the school's elders without a glance, lays a hand on the head of its best young pupil, and the two rise into the light together. Nobody lifts a hand.

choices.text: Watch the sky until it closes

effects.log: The rent seals like a wound. For a breath you see beyond it a hall of pale stone the size of a hill, and then only blue.
The mother sits in the yard holding a pair of small shoes. You sit with her until dark. Neither of you speaks the word god.

choices.text: Ask the elders why they stood still

effects.log: The oldest holds out his hands. They will not stop shaking. "One does not fight the weather," he says. You decide he is wrong.

events.text: The best pupil of the school you lead is at the well when the sky opens. A tall figure in white comes down and looks the youngster over as a buyer looks over a colt, and takes them by the wrist. The elders bow. The pupils bow. The dropped bucket rolls across the flagstones, and you are the only one who hears it.

effects.log: It looks at you for the first time. "Brave," it says, and something lifts you and sets you down inside the well-house. When you come out, they are gone.
You bow. You will think about the bucket for a year.

choices.text: Mark the hour and the sky

effects.log: You write it all down: the hour, the shape of the light, the words it did not trouble to say. Someone will want to know.

events.text: The great bronze bowl of the kingdom's oldest temple, where nine generations of kings burned their first incense, is gone in the morning. In its place lies one white feather and a slip of pale stone: the small gods thank the throne for its gift. The court is already arguing about how to say that the throne gave it.

choices.text: Let them say it was a gift

effects.log: The court calls it a gift. The people call it a theft. Both are right, and you know which will be remembered.
You put the feather in a lacquered box. It is warm when you touch it, as if the bird that shed it is still near.

choices.text: Have the theft written in the annals

effects.log: A brave scribe writes it plain. You see that the ink does not change.

events.text: The famous Moon-Pool sword, kept under glass in the great hall for two hundred years, is taken in the middle of a festival. Thousands see it rise from its case and float up into a cloud that was not there a moment before. A child claps. Then nobody claps.

effects.log: You run until the cloud thins to nothing over the river. On the bank lies the sword's empty scabbard, dropped like a peel.
By evening the taverns say the small gods take what they like now. By midnight they say someone should do something.

choices.text: Go home and sharpen your own blade

effects.log: Your blade will never be the Moon-Pool. It is yours, and it is still here.

events.text: The village of Three Fords would not send the small gods their tithe of grain. Three nights later its fields burn with a fire that falls from a clear sky, row by row, neatly, as if a scribe were crossing lines out of a ledger. Nobody dies. That, everyone agrees, is the message.

choices.text: Help them save the seed grain

effects.log: You carry sacks out of the smoke until your arms give. Half the seed is saved. Next spring Three Fords plants it in ash.
Forty rows, exactly. The small gods can count. So can you.
An old woman spits in the ash. "Every village between here and the sea," she says. "This was the first."

events.text: The tall messenger takes what it came for, and turns to go back up. Then it halts, half in the light, and looks straight at you across the crowd. It frowns the way one frowns at a face from long ago. "You again," it says, though you have never seen it in this life, and is gone.

effects.log: Your heart is pounding as if it remembers something you do not. The gods remember, it seems. So does your soul.
The words come out by themselves. A few people near you step away. A few step closer.

events.text: Old Elder Orun, who has led the Reed School on its hill for sixty years, comes to you alone, at night, without his staff. The schools of the kingdoms have been meeting in secret, he says, and the throne with them. They mean to rise against the small gods who set themselves over the world. "We need someone to hold the rest together," he says. "You have the most quarrels."

effects.log: He smiles in the dark, and the old hand on your shoulder trembles with relief.

choices.text: Ask for a night to think

effects.log: He nods and does not argue. The candle burns down while you stare at your hands.
He thanks you and leaves without his staff, as he came. You have a feeling you have just closed a door.

events.text: Marshal Kess kneels before you in an empty audience hall, the doors barred from inside. The schools mean to rise, he says, and the king is with them, if the king's treasury will be. "I do not ask you to stand with us," he adds. "I ask you to forget where the silver went."

effects.log: You write the first false entry yourself, in your own hand. Your hand is perfectly steady, and that frightens you.

choices.text: Ask what the schools will do with it

effects.log: He tells you plainly: spears, wards, bread. It sounds, you realise, like a sensible request.

choices.text: Refuse him and keep the seal

effects.log: You forbid him to speak of it again. He bows and goes, and the doors seem very heavy as they close behind him.

events.text: A big young farmhand with a broken nose sits down across from you at the inn and slides a pewter ring across the table. Tamsin, he says his name is. The ring is the sign of the Rising. "We are hiring fighters," he says, in the voice of a man hiring fighters for a harvest.

effects.log: It is cold, then warm. You turn it twice on your finger before you understand you have accepted.

choices.text: Ask who the Rising is against

effects.log: "The small gods," he says, "and the ones who kneel to them." He looks at his hands. "I used to be one."
He puts it away without a word, and finishes your ale as well as his own.

events.text: The messenger who brings the call stops at your door and stares. "Forgive me," the messenger says. "You were at the first gathering, long ago. The old songs say a stranger stood with us, and was never seen again. You have the stranger's way of standing."

effects.log: The messenger bursts into tears and then into laughter. You go inside to fetch your coat.

choices.text: Say you are not that stranger

effects.log: You close the door. The messenger does not move for a long time.

events.text: Months after you turned the Rising away, you see Tamsin on the road, or someone with the same broken nose, walking north with a spear and a bundle. He does not see you. You stand in the lane until he is a speck, and then until he is nothing.

effects.log: He turns and lifts a hand. Nothing else passes between you, and nothing needs to.
You let him go. The road keeps its silence, as roads do.
You walk the other way. The wind is against you the whole while.

events.text: A peddler comes through with news from the Ash Gap: the Rising won. The small gods have withdrawn behind their cloud, and the temples of the lowland are being turned into granaries. You were not there. Whatever the world is now, you had no hand in making it.

effects.log: The peddler shrugs. "Loud," he says. "Then very quiet." He accepts a cup of your tea and does not elaborate.
The old temple floor holds sacks of barley now, and nobody has stolen the incense burner. You touch it once.

events.text: News comes on a cold morning: the Rising was crushed at the Ash Gap. Old Elder Orun's school is a field of pale grass, and nobody sings of it. The small gods have taken one of every family's children as a lesson. You were not there, and you do not know whether that is a mercy.

choices.text: Light a candle for the fallen

effects.log: You light it on the sill. It does not flicker. It does not go out.

choices.text: Burn your own copy of the school oath

effects.log: The ash is grey and fine. You pour it onto the lane and the wind takes it.

events.text: You ride three days to a school that has hated yours for a generation, and sit in its hall while its elders shout. By the second morning the shouting has turned to arguing, and by the third to a quiet vote. The Rising has one more school than it had a week ago.

choices.text: Concede the old quarrel in public

effects.log: You bow to their founder's portrait. Their elders look at one another, and the vote goes your way by a single voice.
You trade grain for ward-lore and silence for patience. They are not your friends. They are, tonight, on your side.

events.text: A raid on the small gods' shrine above the lowest ridge is yours to plan: a dozen pupils from four schools, one stair, one night, one ward-stone to bring down. You drill them in the dark with wooden swords until the stair feels like their own.

effects.log: You do. It comes free with a sound like a swallowed word. Your pupils carry it down the stair in a litter, laughing.

choices.text: Send the youngest and keep the oldest in reserve

effects.log: The youngest is too proud to be grateful and too young to fail. The shrine is silent by dawn.

events.text: The shrine's keeper was awake. The raid ends in a scramble down an icefall, a pupil with a sprained wrist carried between two others, the ward-stone left where it lay. No one is lost. Everyone is ashamed. Your pupils look to you to say what it meant.

choices.text: Say it was your plan that failed

effects.log: Their shoulders ease. They are young and they would have followed you into worse.

choices.text: Plan the next one before dawn

effects.log: You do not sleep. By morning there is a chalk map on the floor of the barn, and the pupils crowd around it.

events.text: You hide the Rising inside the ordinary business of a school: a feast day that is really a muster, a pilgrimage that is really a march, a harvest song that is really a roll call. The small gods' watchers attend, politely, and clap in the right places.

choices.text: Teach the pupils to sing it well

effects.log: They sing it so well that the watchers weep a little. The roll call goes by unnoticed.

choices.text: Keep the real roll in your head

effects.log: You commit eight hundred names to memory. It costs you three nights of sleep and no one a thing.

events.text: Silver leaves the treasury by night under false entries: a bridge repaired, a flood relieved, a famine prepared for. The bridge is repaired. The flood is relieved. The famine is not coming, and the grain bought for it is in a barn on a hill.

effects.log: You sign every page. Every signature is a rope you have tied around your own wrist.

choices.text: Have the clerks forget some of the pages

effects.log: The clerks are good at forgetting. The books close with an elegant lack of detail.

events.text: A raid on a waystation of the small gods in the hills: the palace guard, dressed as river-bandits, go in at dusk with ladders and come out at dawn with a chest of tithe-grain and a ward-stone in a basket. The captain returns it to you with a bow and no explanation. You do not ask for one.

effects.log: You find the captain a better horse. Nothing else in the world could say it more clearly.

choices.text: Keep the stone out of the treasury ledger

effects.log: The ledger says nothing about stones. Neither do you.

events.text: The guard returns from the hills with burns that no ordinary fire makes, and without the stone. The captain does not look you in the eye. The small gods will wonder who paid for it. Your physicians treat the burns in the dark, in a closed room, and the room smells of honey.

choices.text: Sit with the wounded through the night

effects.log: They sleep, one by one. The captain stays awake, ashamed, and you stay awake with him.

choices.text: Send them to a far estate to heal

effects.log: The far estate is quiet and nobody will think to ask. You hope.

events.text: You bury the Rising under court business: a commission to study the rivers that never meets, a festival of lamps that costs more than any festival ought, a visiting delegation of philosophers who ask the small gods' stewards sincere and endless questions.

effects.log: They are delighted. The stewards are exhausted. The Rising has not been mentioned once.

choices.text: Let the commission study and study

effects.log: The commission studies the rivers for a year. The rivers, unmoved, flow on.

events.text: You carry sealed letters between schools that would not let each other's messengers through the gate, on foot, in weather. Each letter is a pledge. Each gate you pass is a small risk. You learn to read the faces of gatekeepers as other people read signs.

choices.text: Memorise a letter in case it is lost

effects.log: You do. The letter is not lost. You are a little proud of it all the same.
The long way is wet. It is also empty, and it is yours.

events.text: The raid on the small gods' shrine is fast and ugly and over before the warden understands it has begun. You pull down the ward-pillar with three others, and the dawn sky holds a strange new colour for an hour afterward.

choices.text: Take a splinter of the pillar

effects.log: It is warm in your palm for a day. After that it is just stone, and you keep it anyway.

choices.text: Slip away before the warden wakes

effects.log: You run until the sun is up. Behind you, the sky goes slowly back to blue.

events.text: The raid falls apart in the first breath. The warden's light sweeps the slope, and you run with the rest, down a gully and across a stream and into a wood where no one will follow. You lie on your back under the trees and listen to the others breathing.

choices.text: Count the others in the dark

effects.log: All of them are there. You count twice to be sure and then, because you can, a third time.
You take your own road home, by night, and tell no one which one.

events.text: You lie low for a season: an ordinary job, an ordinary room, an ordinary face. Twice a stranger asks you the Rising's password in a tavern, and twice you pretend not to know it. It is the hardest work you have ever done, and nobody will ever know you did it.

effects.log: You are a better cobbler than you expected. The shoes are sturdy, and the customers return.

choices.text: Keep to your room and wait

effects.log: The room is quiet. The wait is long. You mark the days on the wall in tiny scratches.

events.text: Elder Orun makes tea over a brazier in a cave above his school, where the Rising's leaders meet. He moves slowly now, and tells you without being asked that he has not slept through a night in two years. "Do not tell the others," he says. "Tell me the weather instead."

effects.log: You tell him rain, and cold, and a good wind from the sea. He closes his eyes and listens, like a man hearing a song.
He laughs, the first true laugh you have heard from him in a year, and pours you a second cup.

events.text: Tamsin was a farmhand until the fire fell on Three Fords. Now he carries a woodcutter's axe and a set of promises. He is bad at both, and getting better at the first. He asks you, with great seriousness, whether a person can be brave without being clever.

choices.text: Tell him it is better that way

effects.log: He accepts it as if you had given him a sword. It will be a long time before he stops thinking about it.

choices.text: Tell him to be clever too

effects.log: He nods and takes out a stub of pencil. He is writing it down.

events.text: The Rising needs someone to carry a warding talisman into the heart of a waystation of the small gods. It is a job with a very good chance of not coming back. Tamsin is the only one who has not found a reason to be elsewhere, and he looks at you across the fire as if waiting to be told no.

effects.log: He goes. The talisman is the size of a walnut, and he carries it like a fragile egg.
He argues with you for an hour. In the end you go, and he walks you to the gate and then does not stop.
The talisman stays in its box. Everyone is a little relieved. Nobody says so.

events.text: Lady Ilmara keeps the Rising's purse and its secrets in the back rooms of her cloth-hall, among the dyes and the smell of wet wool. She counts the silver as if every coin were a person. She is, everyone agrees, the most reliable person in the Rising. You are not certain what is nagging at you.

effects.log: You set a boy to sweep her doorstep. He is good at it. He sees things.

choices.text: Trust her with the next purse

effects.log: She counts it twice and writes the sum in a neat, small hand. You feel the warmth of being believed.

choices.text: Ask her what she wants after the Rising

effects.log: "A quiet shop," she says, after a pause that is a little too long. "And a window with some sun in it."

events.text: Tamsin does not come back from the waystation. The talisman went off; the waystation is a crater full of grey birds. In the mess hall that night there is one empty seat at the end of the long table, and no one has the nerve to sit in it.

effects.log: You sit. After a while others sit nearby. The empty seat is not empty any more.

choices.text: Write to the woman at Three Fords

effects.log: You write the letter four times. The fifth you send. It says only what is true.

events.text: The small gods strike back. A market town that sheltered the Rising's couriers wakes to find all its clocks, bells and mill-wheels gone silent, and stays silent for a month. No one is hurt. Everyone is frightened. The fear is the strike.

choices.text: Ring a handbell through the streets

effects.log: The town rings it with you. By the end of the week, every household owns a handbell.
You send the grain by night. The town knows, and does not talk about it.

choices.text: Stay away until the silence ends

effects.log: You stay away. The silence ends in a month, as silences do.

events.text: A white feather is left on a doorstep of the kin, and another on every house that shares the name. The message is clear and unsigned. The feathers are warm to the touch.

choices.text: Hide your kin in the hill country

effects.log: You send them in ones and twos, in the dark, with new names and good boots. By morning the houses are quiet.
They do not burn easily. When they do, the smoke smells of cold air.
You leave them. The wind lifts one and takes it up the street, and another follows.

events.text: The Rising's hall on the river burns in the night, and its records with it, and three of its speakers are gone by morning. The fire was not an accident. The small gods' watchers had the key. Only one person knew where it was kept, and Lady Ilmara's cloth-hall is quiet and neatly locked.

effects.log: You gather them in a barn. They are stunned and thinner than before. By nightfall they have rewritten the roll from memory.
The door is open. The shelves are bare. A single bolt of undyed linen lies on the counter, folded with great care.

choices.text: Say nothing and count the dead

effects.log: You count. The number does not change however you add it.

events.text: Your watcher brings you a letter, taken from a cart on the mountain road that leads nowhere but the clouds. It is in Lady Ilmara's neat hand and addressed to the small gods' stewards. It is a very long letter. It lists names.

choices.text: Show it to the Rising's speakers

effects.log: The speakers read it in silence. Lady Ilmara is sent for, and a long, awful hour begins.
She reads it without a flicker. "A child is a long way from home," she says at last. "I did what I could."
You feed her three names of men who do not exist. The stewards send soldiers to arrest them, and find a barn.

events.text: The Rising gathers at the Ash Gap, the pass where the clouds come lowest. Schools that never shared a bench share a fire. Elder Orun walks the whole length of the camp in the dusk, touching a shoulder here and there, saying the name of every school he passes aloud.

effects.log: You walk with him. He says nothing for three miles, then something about his youth.

choices.text: Sit by a fire and listen

effects.log: The fire hears you say very little, and approves.

events.text: The throne's last silver goes to the Ash Gap in carts guarded by men in plain clothes. You sit alone in the audience hall with the doors open for the first time in a year. The hall is very large. The kingdom is very small. You think of the Maker, who made it, and wonder whether the Maker is watching.

choices.text: Light every lamp in the hall

effects.log: The hall blazes. It is, for an hour, the brightest place for a hundred miles.
You sleep better than you have in a month. It is, perhaps, the whole point of being king's counsel.

events.text: Around the fire at the Ash Gap nobody sleeps. Somebody has a flute. Somebody has a story about their mother's soup. Somebody laughs too loudly, and everyone is grateful. At the edge of the firelight, someone is writing a letter to a person they will not send it to.

effects.log: You play it badly. Three people join in, worse. It is the finest music in the world for that hour.
You write it, fold it, and put it in your boot. Whoever finds it will be glad of it.

events.text: The cloud over the Ash Gap tears open at dawn, and the small gods come down, and the Rising meets them. By noon it is over. The tall messenger kneels in the dust and the white banner is lowered. Elder Orun puts down his staff and sits on a rock and weeps, plainly, like a child.

effects.log: You sit. After a while he stops weeping and starts laughing, and the laughter spreads down the pass.
You carry the first sack up the temple steps. The steps, which were made for incense, hold the weight.

events.text: The Rising wins at the Ash Gap, and Elder Orun does not live to see it. He fell sleeping the night before, in his tent, with his staff beside him and his tea gone cold. The pass is taken in his name. Someone has laid his straw hat on the topmost stone.

choices.text: Say his name at the pass

effects.log: You say it. The wind carries it to the schools, and then to the towns, and then, you suppose, to the small gods.
It smells of tea and wood-smoke. You hang it by your door and it keeps the draught out.

events.text: Under a white cloth on the scorched pass, the tall messenger and the Rising's speakers sit knee to knee and sign. The small gods will come down only when invited; the kingdoms will not raise their wards against the sky. Nobody has won. Nobody, you realise, has lost, and the silence afterward is so large that it seems to breathe.

effects.log: You sign your name small. It is a stranger signature than you expected, for a moment of such size.
You pour for the messenger first, and then for the speakers. The messenger takes the cup in both hands, with a look of wonder.

events.text: The cloud over the Ash Gap opens, and the light that comes down is not a battle. It is a verdict. The Rising stands in the pass, and the pass is empty a moment later, and the wind is warm. The small gods leave the fields green and the schools silent, and take with them what they came for.

effects.log: You walk it end to end. Your boots find a small, cold ring in the dust, and you pocket it.
You plant barley in a corner of the yard. The barley comes up, as barley does.

events.text: You sold the Rising on the night before its battle. By morning the camp is empty, its fires cold, its banners folded in the river. The small gods keep their word and give you what you asked for, and what you asked for is very little compared to what it cost.

effects.log: You go, and the road is empty, and the reward is exactly what was promised, to the last grain.

choices.text: Go to the river and look at the banners

effects.log: The banners drift in the current, one after another, turning. You count them. There are eleven.

events.text: Every year on the day of the battle, the people of the kingdoms climb to the Ash Gap with bread and lamps, and leave them on the rocks. They do not give speeches. They sit, and break the bread, and when the lamps burn low someone sings. You are asked to say a few words, and find you have none.

choices.text: Say the one word you have

effects.log: You say a name, and the name is answered by four hundred voices.
You break it, and it is warm, and the day goes quietly on.

events.text: In a mountain village you find a school where children learn the Rising's warding patterns as other children learn their letters. The teacher is nervous. The small gods' stewards come by every season to check. They find only children drawing circles, and go away unsatisfied.

effects.log: You teach one. The children are quick, and one of them corrects you politely.

choices.text: Pay the school's rent for a year

effects.log: You leave a small purse in the teacher's shoe. Nobody ever finds out who did.

events.text: A blind storyteller in a market sings the ballad of the night the Rising was sold. She does not name the seller. The crowd leans in, quietly, and watches the faces of everyone near them. The song ends, and the silence goes on, and someone drops a coin in her bowl.

choices.text: Drop a coin in her bowl

effects.log: It rings in the silence. She tilts her head, and sings the last verse again for you alone.
You leave. The song follows you to the corner and a street beyond that.

events.text: A messenger of the small gods comes down to buy cloth in your town, of all things, and stops dead in the street. "I know your face," it says, in a thin voice. "From the Ash Gap. You held the pass." It does not look afraid. It looks a little relieved.

choices.text: Say it was a long time ago

effects.log: The messenger nods and buys the cloth. At the shop door it turns and bows, quite deeply.

choices.text: Ask how the small gods fare

effects.log: "Quieter," it says, "and more careful." It almost smiles.

events.text: You dream of a night you have never lived: a camp emptying, banners going down a river, an old man with a staff sitting alone and looking at the water. In the dream you are the one who left. You wake with the taste of cold tea in your mouth.

choices.text: Say his name aloud, though you do not know it

effects.log: The name comes, from nowhere, and fits your mouth as if you had always known it.
You almost succeed. The tea-taste stays all day.

events.text: The call comes from a mouth you did not expect: a hooded speaker of the Lampless Lodge, the night-school the kingdoms hunt. The speaker bows like a trader and talks like a priest. "The day-schools asked us to stand beside them," the speaker says. "Think of it. The small gods took one of ours as well. For once the whole world has been handed the same enemy."

effects.log: The speaker laughs inside the hood. "Strange days," the speaker says. "Good ones, perhaps."
You listen. You promise nothing. The speaker seems to have expected exactly that.
The speaker bows again. "When they take one of yours," the speaker says, "the offer stands."

events.text: The small gods come for your school. Not with fire: with an invitation. Three of its most gifted pupils are asked up through the cloud as guests, all at once, each by name. Nobody has ever come home from being a guest.

effects.log: They go into the hills under borrowed names. The invitation is answered by an empty hall.
Two hide. One goes up laughing, sure the stories are wrong. You hope the stories are wrong.

events.text: On the night before the battle you climb alone to the lip of the Ash Gap. The cloud hangs so low above you that you could touch it. Somewhere inside it the small gods are making speeches of their own. Your strength, after all these years, is very nearly theirs.

choices.text: Reach up and touch the cloud

effects.log: It is cold, and it parts round your hand like water. On the far side, something stops to listen.

choices.text: Go back down to the fires

effects.log: Down there are the people you are fighting for. You would sooner spend tonight with them.

events.text: The battle of the Ash Gap is won without you. A rider tells you, too out of breath to dismount: the small gods have gone back up through the cloud, and the Rising holds the pass. Your name stands on the roll of those who built it, and not on the roll of those who stood there at the end.

effects.log: You come in time to help carry the wounded down. It is not nothing.

choices.text: Raise a cup where you are

effects.log: You raise your cup to them alone, and pour it out on the ground. It is the best wine you have, and you wish the day had cost less.

events.text: The Rising met the small gods at the Ash Gap without you, and lost. You hear it from the ones coming back along the road: the banners taken down, the names read out from the sky. Some of them look at you as they pass. Not one of them stops.

effects.log: Your house fills with the hurt and the tired. Nobody asks where you were. You tell them anyway.
You walk until the road is empty. It does not help.

events.text: The small gods keep their word. On the empty road out of the camp a light comes down on you alone, and something in you opens that has been shut for a hundred years. You are stronger than you have ever been. Behind you the fires of the Rising go out, one after another.

effects.log: You keep your eyes on the road. The new strength hums in you. It does not warm you.
You see the Ash Gap, and the river with the banners in it, and one lamp somebody has left burning. Then the road bends.

events.text: After the battle the tall messenger comes to your door itself. It has not come for you. It takes someone you love by the hand, kindly, and says they will be an honoured guest of the small gods for as long as you behave. Then the two of them rise into the light, and the door is only a door again.

effects.log: You kneel until the light is gone. You will behave. You will hate every day of it.
The sky does not answer. It did not answer the Rising either.

events.text: The tall messenger comes down once, years after the truce, by invitation, to a school's harvest feast. It sits at the high table, eats one pear and watches the dancing. On the way out it stops beside you. "It is very loud down here," it says, almost fondly.

choices.text: Say: you get used to it

effects.log: It thinks about that. "I do not believe we would," it says, and goes.

choices.text: Ask after the pupils they took

effects.log: "Grown," it says. "Some of them ask about you."
